title: Contributors
Front Matter
The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
authors: Patricia Satterstrom; Michaela Kerrissey
affiliations: New York University, Wagner, New York, New York, United States; Harvard University T H Chan School of Public Health, Health Policy and Management, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence and by characterizing its mirage.

title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
authors: Arzi Adbi; Xiaoteng Wu
affiliations: National University of Singapore Business School, Strategy & Policy, Singapore, Singapore; Peking University Guanghua School of Management, Organization and Strategic Management, Beijing, China
abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with multinational spread reduce emissions intensity of production and increase asset utilization at their clean (electric arc furnace) plants relative to dirty plants. Our study thus sheds light on how firms pursue different adaptation strategies at production facilities in response to carbon taxation.

title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
authors: Jung-Hyun Suh; J.P. Eggers
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Management, Shatin, New Territories, Hong Kong; New York University, Stern School, Mgmt & Orgs, New York, New York, United States
abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights into how incumbents may struggle to use alliances for adaptive learning during the pre-commercialization phase of a new technology.

title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
authors: G. Alessandra Alessandra Rizzi; Vilmos F. Misangyi
affiliations: Texas Christian University, Management and Leadership, Fort Worth, Texas, United States; The Pennsylvania State University, Department of Management & Organization, University Park, Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 S&P 500 CEOs across 45 ideologically polarized U.S. media outlets between 2016 and 2022, we find broad support for our hypotheses across our main and extensive supplemental analyses. Our findings advance understanding of CEO infamy and social evaluations more generally by revealing how partisan media construct divergent social evaluations of the same executive behavior through distinct narrative processes.

title: Can Voluntary Corporate Transparency Curb Corruption? Community-Level Evidence from Oil and Gas Fields in Africa
authors: Shirley Tang; Daniel W Elfenbein; Tatenda M Pasipanodya
affiliations: Boston University, Strategy and Innovation, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; Washington University in St Louis, John M. Olin School of Business, St. Louis, Missouri, United States; Louisiana State University System, Management, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, United States
abstract: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits. We examine whether this form of self-regulation can help curb corruption where formal oversight is weak, focusing on corporate support for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI), a multistakeholder initiative that promotes disclosure of company payments to host governments. We link geolocated data on African oil and gas fields and their operators to Afrobarometer surveys and satellite nighttime-light measures and estimate difference-in-differences models that track changes in outcomes around the same fields before and after operators endorse the EITI. We find that corporate EITI support is associated with lower perceived corruption and less reported bribery, greater civic engagement, greater perceived freedom to speak, and higher nighttime-light intensity, a proxy for local economic activity. The association with lower perceived corruption is stronger around fields with nearby NGO or aid-project activity, among residents living closer to fields, and among frequent users of traditional news media. Supplementary analyses provide indirect evidence that supporting firms were more transparent before mandatory disclosure laws took effect, and show that they had fewer joint-venture partners and larger ownership stakes after endorsement. Archival cases from Nigeria and Ghana illustrate how civil-society organizations and journalists use extractive-industry information to question firms and public authorities. The findings point to local governance benefits of voluntary transparency commitments and are consistent with an information-to-accountability account in which these benefits depend on both substantive reporting and local opportunities to scrutinize and use the information.

title: The Complexity of Scheduling Pickup and Delivery Jobs
authors: Tianyu Wang; Desheng Wu; David L. Olson
affiliations: Beihang University, School of Economy and Management, Beijing, Beijing, China; UCAS, School of Economy and Management, Beijing, China; Lincoln, United States
abstract: Scheduling pickup and delivery jobs stands as a critical and challenging problem commonly encountered in time-sensitive logistics and transportation. Often, a large number of requests involving shipments from the same location are aggregated into either a fixed number of job queues, referred to as the queueing mode, or into a fixed number of sets, referred to as the pooling mode. Due to the time-sensitive nature, the objective of scheduling jobs by location and routing drivers is to minimize customers’ waiting times. While request aggregation is widely observed in platform economies and related research, the computational complexity of scheduling pickup and delivery jobs has not been studied. This paper presents a comprehensive complexity analysis of this problem. We prove that the problem is strongly NP-hard in the queueing mode, but is polynomially solvable in the pooling mode. Furthermore, we prove that both modes become polynomially solvable when minimizing total distance, as does the queueing mode with fixed number of drivers or scaled-length edges. Finally, we provide approximation guarantees and extend the analysis to bipartite graphs, identifying solvable variants with relaxed map-size constraints to enhance the applicability.

title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
authors: Yuefeng Li; Zhongbin Wang; Shenghai Zhou
affiliations: School of Economics and Management, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China; College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China; School of Business, Central South University, Changsha, Hunan 410083, China; and Laboratory of Intelligent Governance for Complex Social Systems, Changsha, Hunan 410083, China
abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
authors: Matthew Jaremski; Kris James Mitchener; Kilian Rieder
affiliations: Department of Economics and Finance, Huntsman School of Business, Utah State University & NBER, Logan, Utah 84322; Department of Economics, Leavey School of Business, Santa Clara University, NBER, CEPR, CESifo & CAGE, Santa Clara, California 95053; Economics and Research Department, Oesterreichische Nationalbank (Eurosystem) & CEPR, Vienna 1090, Austria
abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
authors: Tianyu Wang; Jiashuo Liu; Peng Cui; Hongseok Namkoong
affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Department of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100190, China; Decision, Risk, and Operations Division, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
authors: Chamsi Hssaine; Sean R. Sinclair
affiliations: Department of Data Sciences and Operations, University of Southern California, Marshall School of Business, Los Angeles, California 90089; Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
authors: Yanjun (Penny) Liao; Philip Mulder
affiliations: Resources for the Future, Washington, District of Columbia 20036; Department of Risk and Insurance, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53715
abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
authors: Shamim Ahmed; Cesare Robotti; Daniel Tsvetanov; Xiaoxia Ye
affiliations: University of Liverpool Management School, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 7ZH, United Kingdom; Warwick Business School, University of Warwick, Coventry CV4 7AL, United Kingdom; Norwich Business School, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, United Kingdom; Nottingham University Business School, University of Nottingham, Nottingham NG8 1BB, United Kingdom
abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
authors: Benjamin Knox; Jakob Ahm Sørensen
affiliations: Division of International Finance, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, District of Columbia 20551; Finance Department, Bocconi University, Milan 20136, Italy
abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. title: The Workplace GenAI Usage Divide: A Genetics-Informed Cognitive and Metacognitive Account
authors: Shuhua Sun; Shiyang Gong; Yinliang (Ricky) Tan
affiliations: Tulane University Freeman School of Business, Management, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States; Beijing Normal University, Business School, Beijing, China; China Europe International Business School, Freeman School of Business, Shanghai, China
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our model using a multisource dataset combining primary genetic data, survey measures, and 21 months of objective usage logs. The results show that educational attainment PGS, a broad distal genetic index, is associated with both GenAI use frequency and interaction intensity and provide theory-consistent evidence for the proposed pathways. Overall, our study offers a micro-foundational account of the persistent GenAI usage divide and advances IS theory on the use of probabilistic, general-purpose systems in the workplace.

title: Spatial Competition in Fast-Charging Networks
authors: Philipp Artur Artur Kienscherf; Yixin Lu; Long He; Wolfgang Ketter
affiliations: University of Cologne, Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, Koln, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Germany; The George Washington University, School of Business, Washington, District of Columbia, United States; University of Notre Dame Mendoza College of Business, Information Technology, Analytics, and Operations, Notre Dame, Indiana, United States
abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers. To overcome tractability issues associated with large networks that arise from real-world settings, we propose a computationally efficient method to optimize CPOs’ pricing decisions. We instantiate the framework in Germany’s Deutschlandnetz, whose awarded regional network comprises 900 charging stations. Using demand projections for 2030, we conduct a series of counterfactual simulations. Our analysis generates four sets of findings. First, price exhibits a strong negative correlation with the local competitiveness level (measured by the density of charging stations), but shows no clear dependence on absolute demand levels. Second, CPOs’ profits are shaped by both local competitiveness and absolute demand. Third, a uniform, stringent price cap may create inefficiencies in network utilization and discourage infrastructure investment, particularly in less lucrative regions. Finally, spatial and ownership constraints in tender rules may fail to ensure competitive outcomes in large-scale charging networks, allowing CPOs to strategically select locations that strengthen their market power ex post. Taken together, these findings suggest that policymakers should enable regionally equitable access to fast charging while ensuring efficient network utilization.

title: EXPRESS: Benefits of Extreme Political Stability and Instability of Supplier Countries for Firms: The U-Shaped Relationship
authors: Jafar Namdar; Sachin Modi; Arash Azadegan; Milad Baghersad
abstract: Using a large-scale panel dataset of U.S. buyer firms and their global supplier networks from 2010 to 2020, we examine how global political instability (GPI), a firm’s weighted exposure to political instability across the countries where its international suppliers operate, is associated with firm performance. We find a U-shaped relationship: buyer firm performance is highest when a firm's overall sourcing exposure reflects either very low or very high levels of GPI. At the low-GPI end, the results align with transaction-cost economics (TCE), as political stability is associated with lower uncertainty and fewer coordination frictions. At the very high-GPI end, we identify bargaining power as a key mechanism: buyers exposed to politically unstable supplier countries exhibit greater bargaining power and more favorable contractual terms, particularly favorable trade credit, which may partially offset the costs of political instability. We further show that this nonlinear relationship varies across industries. It is more pronounced in productive industries, where buyers have greater bargaining power to negotiate favorable trade credit and lower switching costs to reallocate sourcing during periods of political instability. However, it is flatter in durable-goods industries, where asset specificity and higher switching costs are associated with weaker bargaining power and a more limited ability to secure favorable trade credit from suppliers in politically unstable countries. Finally, we document an important managerial trade-off: while higher exposure to unstable supplier countries is associated with improved performance, it is also associated with more negative media coverage related to supply chain issues and ethical risks. Our results remain robust across multiple complementary identification strategies, strengthening confidence that the documented nonlinear effect and its underlying mechanism are not driven by spurious correlations or a single empirical approach.

title: EXPRESS: Dynamic Principal-Agent Problem in Queueing Systems with Customer Abandonment
authors: Tan Yu; Tiaojun Xiao; Xiang Zhong; Xiaohan Zhu
abstract: Service systems in which demand, congestion, and worker incentives evolve jointly are ubiquitous in modern operations. We study a dynamic principal–agent problem in a queueing system with customer abandonment, where the principal controls arrivals through pricing and the agent privately chooses a costly service rate. Modeling workload as a controlled reflected diffusion, we characterize the centralized and decentralized Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and construct a representative two-part contract consisting of an access charge and a completion payment. Under unrestricted transfers, the contract coordinates pricing and service to attain the first-best joint payoff. Whenever participation is feasible, it makes the agent's participation constraint bind and allocates the remaining surplus to the principal. Implementation is robust to misspecification of the service-rate function used by the principal. We also establish conditions under which the representative payment schedules are nonmonotone in workload. Extensions consider multiple agents, general patience distributions, and information disclosure in a reduced Bayesian-persuasion benchmark. Numerical examples illustrate how the effects of customer impatience on optimal pricing and service can vary with congestion.

title: EXPRESS: Digital Platforms Meet Artificial Intelligence: Implications for POM Research and Practice
authors: Edward Anderson; Nitin Joglekar; Sunil Mithas; Geoffrey Parker; Yinliang (Ricky) Tan
abstract: Digital platforms are changing how firms design, coordinate, and govern operations by integrating artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital sensing and digital twins, data infrastructure, and additive manufacturing. This paper develops a forward-looking research agenda for production and operations management by distinguishing enabling technologies from the platforms, workflows, and business models through which they are deployed. We organize the agenda around a sequence linking technological capability, operational manifestation, mechanism, outcomes, and boundary conditions. The relevant mechanisms include prediction, information visibility, verification, orchestration, monitoring, human override, and decision rights. We articulate how these mechanisms may create operational value through improvements in productivity, quality, responsiveness, resilience, compliance, and customer experience, enabling firms to capture financial value through revenue growth, cost reduction, risk avoidance, and improved asset utilization. We identify enduring operations management themes that emerging technologies may reshape, and develop five forward-looking paths involving artificial intelligence-enabled business-to-business platforms, physical–digital integration, agentic service workflows, data and artificial intelligence governance, and platform-enabled resilience under geopolitical disruption. Finally, we discuss theoretical and methodological approaches that can support cumulative research.

title: EXPRESS: An Exploratory Analysis of Variation in Payback Periods of Emissions Reduction Projects Using CDP Disclosures
authors: Christian C. Blanco; Felipe Caro; Charles J. Corbett
abstract: Firms continue to engage in projects to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Based on their disclosures to CDP, many such projects have relatively short payback periods of 2-3 years. Earlier work by Blanco et al. (2020) found that payback periods appeared stable over time between 2010-2016. The current paper extends that work in several directions: by using a substantially longer time horizon, and exploring several factors that contribute to the variation in payback periods and trends. With the longer horizon of data now available, we find that paybacks are lengthening slowly but significantly over 2010-2024, by an average of about 2 weeks per year, or approximately one half year over our 14-year horizon. Firms with greater liabilities relative to their assets report faster payback, though the effect is only marginally significant. Firms in Europe that are subject to a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme report shorter paybacks than in the US or elsewhere. Firms that are more consumer-facing report lengthening payback periods, while upstream firms do not. This analysis is exploratory, but prior firm-level research on these effects is mixed and surprisingly limited.

title: EXPRESS: Bounded Rationality in Public Healthcare Competition
authors: Yu Zhang; Hao Wu; Zhongbin Wang
abstract: Fiscal pressure forces public healthcare systems to reduce waiting times via hospital competition, yet patients' bounded rationality weakens this policy. We develop a Hotelling-type queueing model that incorporates the strategic interaction between two budget-constrained public hospitals and patients with heterogeneous preferences and bounded rationality. Our analysis yields the following results. First, we show that bounded rationality can incentivize hospitals to increase service rates, thereby alleviating congestion and leading to an inverted-U relationship between patient welfare and the degree of bounded rationality. Moreover, the effect of bounded rationality on hospital revenue is also non-monotonic: when the capacity constraint is tight and the budget is sufficiently high, hospital revenue may be maximized at an intermediate level of bounded rationality rather than under full rationality. Second, higher reimbursement does not necessarily enhance patient welfare; instead, we identify an optimal reimbursement level that rises with the available public budget. Third, extending the framework to a multi-hospital environment within a Salop model shows that total market share, patient welfare, and hospital revenue are all maximized at a moderate level of competition. Overall, from a managerial perspective, healthcare managers should carefully account for patients' bounded rationality when designing capacity and information disclosure policies. Meanwhile, excessive hospital expansion may undermine both operational efficiency and financial sustainability. We further confirm the robustness of our main insights under alternative objectives (profit maximization and social welfare), systematic bias, heterogeneous hospital objectives, and other cost specifications.

title:
The Interplay of Digital and Physical Materialities in
                    <scp>IT</scp>
                    Affordances: A Study of Governance of Controlled Medications in a Hospital
authors: Valentina Lichtner; Ela Klecun
affiliations: School of Health Sciences University of Manchester Manchester UK; London School of Economics London UK
abstract: ABSTRACT In studies of information technology (IT) in organizations, affordance theory may be used to explain what possibilities for action IT offers, under what conditions they are actualized and how they shape action and outcomes. Affordance theory suggests that materiality matters because it furnishes possibilities for action. However, in studies of IT affordances, the digital and physical materialities of IT are usually in focus, while the physical materiality of non‐IT artefacts is seldom considered. This paper examines how the physical materiality of non‐IT artefacts conditions the action possibilities an IT system offers its users. We base our observations on a study of IT implemented in a hospital to improve visibility and accountability of the use of controlled drugs, such as opioids. We compare how the materiality of both IT and paper‐based systems used for these purposes interplays with the materiality of the medications and other non‐IT artefacts in nurses and pharmacists' accountability work. We found different combinations of technologies and medications, condition visibility for the organization in different ways, with distinct ways of knowing about medication work, and different potential accountability outcomes. Temporal processes of accountability work, such as recurrence, accumulation or temporal lag, also condition different outcomes of affordance actualization. Overall, by illuminating material and temporal influences behind visibility and potential for accountability afforded by IT to organizations we deepen the understanding of the action potential afforded by IT and reveal opportunities for redesign of technology and organizational processes.

title: AI and Stress
authors: Thang Dang; Phuong Huynh
affiliations: Department of Economics University of Turku Turku Finland; University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City (UEH) Ho Chi Minh City Vietnam; University of Turku Turku Finland
abstract: ABSTRACT Given the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) tools at work, understanding their health implications is critically important. We use rich survey data from Finland and apply propensity score matching that accounts for observable differences between regular AI users and non‐users to estimate the relationship between reported AI usage at work and workers’ reported stress. Regular AI use is associated with a 4.4 percentage point higher probability of reporting stress, equivalent to a 25.6% increase relative to baseline. Comparing two competing explanations, we find that this pattern is more consistent with heavier work demands than with concerns about job loss: AI use is associated with more unpaid work outside working hours and, less precisely, with intense work absorption, but not with job insecurity. Exploratory subgroup estimates are larger and individually significant for men, non‐supervisors, unionized workers and employees in medium‐sized workplaces, although the differences across subgroups are not statistically significant.

title: ‘The More We Could Be Involved in Stuff, the More Effective It'd Be’: The Need for More Employer Involvement in Active Labour Market Policy
authors: Katy Jones; Sharlene Farrugia
affiliations: Manchester Metropolitan University Manchester UK
abstract: ABSTRACT While internationally, interest has grown in employer engagement with active labour market policy (ALMP), their involvement in policy development has been limited—especially in liberal market economies, which lack the institutional frameworks and traditions of social partnership observed elsewhere. Applying a social dialogue lens to interviews with 124 employers, policymakers and other social actors in the UK context, we consider its potential expressive and instrumental functions, and the extent to which facilitating conditions exist to enable it. As in‐work poverty and poor job quality present key intractable challenges for policymakers at national and local levels, we present a revival in social dialogue in ALM policymaking as a critical factor for preventing institutional failure and unlocking innovative policy solutions, especially where supporting people to access and progress in ‘good work’ is a policy priority.

title:
Explaining Coexisting Trust and Distrust Transitions: The Case of Senior Doctors in the
                    <scp>UK NHS</scp>
authors: Branko Božič; Stacey Bushfield; Graeme Martin
affiliations: NEOMA Business School; Edinburgh Napier University Business School; University of Dundee School of Business
abstract: Abstract The emergence of distrust in organizations damages working relationships and leads to poor organizational performance. We examine how senior doctors in the UK NHS transitioned from low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust in their managers and employer. Drawing on qualitative data from three time periods, we show, counter‐intuitively, how a positive crisis response by doctors' leaders during COVID‐19 intensified a long‐term downward trust–distrust trajectory. This response temporarily restored confidence and elevated expectations of a renewed psychological contract among doctors. When those expectations were later violated, scepticism and value incongruence grew, inciting negative expectations and a descent into distrust. We make three contributions to trust–distrust theory. First, we identify a previously unexplained pathway from coexisting low trust/low distrust to low trust/high distrust through a temporary state of high trust/low distrust. Second, we explain how ideological contract violations, perceived betrayals of core values and professional identities, drive the development of distrust. Third, we extend punctuated‐threshold explanations of distrust emergence by demonstrating that distrust can arise not only from accumulating negative experiences but also from the collapse of newly restored positive expectations. This has broader implications for the leadership of change, particularly the management of hope and expectations during crisis.

title: Constant Connectivity as Everyday Practice: Theorizing Through Problematization
authors: Matthew B. Perrigino; Roshni Raveendhran; Ji Woon Ryu
affiliations: Baruch College; University of Virginia; Portland State University
abstract: Abstract Despite a significant amount of research on constant connectivity , defined as the opportunity to remain connected to work at any time, from any place, we assert that there remains a disconnect between how constant connectivity is studied and how it unfolds in everyday occurrences. Using the miner‐prospector continuum, we problematize the extant literature to evaluate this assertion and develop new theory. Our mining reveals that constant connectivity studies rely on notions of time and place that insufficiently demarcate work–nonwork boundaries; prescribe constant connectivity as either wholly incompatible with enacting nonwork roles or inherently interfering with specific nonwork activities; and operationalize constant connectivity with vague ‘technology use’ constructs. In prospecting, we conceptualize constant connectivity as a set of sociomaterial practices that capture how: technology affords opportunities to engage in, and disengage from, work activity; constant connectivity and nonwork role enactment are compatible via the pursuit of work and nonwork activities in parallel or sequentially; and work–nonwork boundaries are socially constructed in ways that transcend time and place. Taken together, we extend considerations of constant connectivity beyond knowledge workers to any occupation (skilled trades; physical labour) in which individuals use technology to conduct aspects of work at any time, from any place.

title: Exploring the Dark Side of the Coopetition Paradox: Unintentional Knowledge Leakage, Capital Structure, and Organizational Decline in Small‐Firm Coopetition
authors: Tatbeeq Raza‐Ullah; Saouré Kouamé; Baback Yazdani
affiliations: Nottingham Business School; Telfer School of Management
abstract: Abstract While paradox theory's generative view implicitly assumes that actors possess the agency to navigate contradictory pursuits productively, an emerging dark‐side perspective suggests that power relations and material constraints may transform such pursuits into pragmatic paradoxes. Building on this perspective, we explore how constrained paradox navigation manifests in behavioural dysfunction and contributes to organizational decline. We study this process in small‐firm coopetition, where boundary‐spanning managers experience the paradoxical tension of coopetition while juggling persistent, contradictory demands. We propose that this tension is positively associated with unintentional knowledge leakage (UKL), a boundary‐regulation failure whereby managers inadvertently disclose sensitive knowledge to a competing partner. In turn, UKL relates to organizational decline, thereby mediating the tension–decline relationship, while capital structure (financial leverage) amplifies the tension–UKL association. Using survey and archival data from 236 Swedish small technology‐manufacturing firms, we find support for these relationships. We advance paradox theory by identifying boundary‐regulation failure as a distinct dark‐side dysfunction and financial leverage as a material boundary condition that exacerbates the constraining effects of paradox navigation. We also reorient coopetition research from intentional partner appropriation toward inadvertent disclosure by the focal firm's own managers. Practically, we highlight the importance of financial resilience in preserving managers' discretion when navigating coopetition's dark side.

title: Rigorous Engaged Scholarship
authors: Amanda Williams; Ali Aslan Gümüşay; Andrew J. Hoffman
affiliations: Emlyon Business School; LMU Munich and Humboldt Institute for Internet & Society Berlin; University of Michigan
abstract: Abstract Scholars are increasingly asked to address societal grand challenges. Yet forms of scholarship that pursue these aims through engagement with practice are often treated with suspicion. In this Point, we intend to zoom in on this paradox. We argue that engaged scholarship requires rethinking what it means to be rigorous when working closely with practitioners. We advance this conversation by defining a novel set of six principles to guide its rigor: articulating positionality, orienting prospectively, collaborating critically, experimenting systematically, appearing visibly, and reflecting inwardly. These principles enhance current norms in management studies regarding knowledge production, leading us to suggest how the institutional environment will need to change to support rigorous engaged scholarship.

title: The French touch: Product quality and France's great trade liberalization, 1850–74
authors: Stéphane Becuwe; Bertrand Blancheton; Dan Liu; Christopher M. Meissner
affiliations: University of Bordeaux Bordeaux France; Liaoning University Shenyang China; University of California Davis California USA; NBER Cambridge Massachusetts USA
abstract: Abstract We explore changes in product quality during France's major liberalization episode of the mid‐nineteenth century. Using new data and existing techniques from the international trade literature, we investigate the relative quality of French products versus those of international competitors, within‐industry changes in quality, and within‐product quality changes. France produced relatively high‐quality, high unit value products in the traded sector throughout the period. Liberalization was associated with an overall decline in the quality of French exports. However, some of the best‐selling exports experienced an apparent rise in quality around the time of liberalization. As for imports, whilst French spending may have switched to lower‐quality products due to liberalization, lower tariffs were associated with rising within‐product quality.

title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
authors: Kevin Smith
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)
